answer_text: Faraday explains that the cup forms because an ascending current of air plays regularly on all sides of the candle, keeping the exterior cool so the outside wax does not melt, while only the fuel near the wick melts and is drawn up in small quantities to burn. The only reason the candle does not burn all down the side of the wick is that the melted tallow extinguishes the flame, since fuel running onto the wick has not had time to be heated enough to burn, unlike the fuel carried up in small quantities where the heat has full effect. If the current of air is irregular, the cup is badly formed and the candle gutters, because gravity keeps the fluid horizontal and it runs away if the cup is not level. No fuel would serve for a candle that cannot form this cup, except material like Irish bogwood, which is sponge-like and holds its own fuel.

Faraday says Benjamin Franklin's father made candles of tallow, and tallow is made from the suet—the fat of the ox (Russian tallow)—as described in the candle lecture on the flame's sources. It can be turned into stearin through the work of Gay Lussac (or someone entrusted with his knowledge), who converted the suet/tallow into that beautiful substance, stearin.
